summary: CDAS combines a Jensen–Shannon distribution-matching objective with distributed interchange interventions for bi-directional LLM steering, motivated by causal localization rather than strong Lang./PO supervision. The idea is coherent and the safety case studies (refusal override, CoT backdoor) show a credible utility-preservation advantage, but AXBENCH evidence is mixed and often depends on post-hoc factor scaling that undercuts the “faithful / unit-factor” narrative. Relative to the ICLR bar, the contribution is promising but still incremental and under-ablated, so acceptance would require stronger isolation of components, fairer baseline protocols, and clearer statistical support.
strengths: Clear conceptual framing that treats steering as identifying and manipulating concept features, with an explicit weak-supervision alternative to Lang./PO objectives.
Method is concrete: contrastive DII protocol, full-vocabulary JSD matching, and a principled (if imperfect) unit-factor story at inference.
Safety case studies are well chosen and show CDAS can suppress refusal/backdoor behavior while better preserving benchmarks and KL to the model’s natural distribution than tuned RePS.
Calibration is relatively honest: the paper admits it does not always beat strong-supervised methods, lists data/factor/rank limitations, and reports both oracle and fair AXBENCH scores.

key_concerns.issue: General-purpose claims are weakly supported: on Gemma-2-2B CDAS trails RePS/Lang., on Gemma-2-9B it wins only at one layer, and the principled unit-factor setting is substantially weaker than tuned β scaling—undermining the faithfulness/DII-factor story for the main benchmark.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Either narrow claims to utility-critical / large-model suppression settings, or add decisive general-purpose evidence (more models/layers, stronger unit-factor results, and head-to-head protocols where all methods use comparable factor-selection budgets).

key_concerns.issue: Component isolation is incomplete: DAS (Lang.+DII) partially separates the objective, but there is no clean ablation of JSD vs KL/CE under the same DII protocol, nor JSD under addition/clamping without DII, so it is unclear what drives gains.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Add a factorial ablation (objective × intervention protocol × factor policy) on AXBENCH and at least one case study, with the same data and selection budgets.

key_concerns.issue: Baseline comparison fairness is uneven across sections (RePS factor-tuned; CDAS unit-factor in case studies; DIM untuned; BiPO weak on AXBENCH without clear tuning parity), making complementary-advantage conclusions hard to trust.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Report a single fair protocol table: identical search budgets for inference factors, shared layers/tokens where possible, and sensitivity curves vs. factor strength for all methods.

key_concerns.issue: Statistical rigor is below typical accepted ML venue standards outside the backdoor SE shades: refusal results lack multi-seed variance, AXBENCH improvements lack significance tests, and tinyBenchmarks (100 examples) are thin for utility claims on 70B-scale interventions.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Report means±stderr over ≥3 seeds for all main tables, bootstrap or paired tests on fair AXBENCH splits, and larger utility suites (full MMLU/ARC or equivalent) for the backdoor setting.

key_concerns.issue: Naming and positioning risk confusion: calling the Lang.+DII baseline “DAS” while stressing that CDAS is not causal variable localization blurs contribution boundaries relative to Geiger et al.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Rename the Lang.+DII baseline and sharpen Related Work to state what is borrowed from DAS versus what is new for steering.

questions_for_authors: With matched factor-search budgets, does unit-factor or lightly scaled CDAS still beat RePS/Lang. on any AXBENCH setting, or is tuning essential for competitiveness?
How much of the case-study win is due to JSD versus DII versus the specific source-token / clamping choices?
Why does CDAS fail to suppress refusal on Phi-3.5-mini while succeeding on Llama-3.1-8B/70B—scale, layer choice, or data mismatch?
For AXBENCH, how sensitive are fair scores to the gpt-4o-mini augmentation that creates the contrastive pairs CDAS/PO need but Lang. does not?
Does replacing JSD with forward/reverse KL or token-level CE under identical DII training recover or destroy the KL/utility benefits?
calibration_check: Claims of a more stable, causally motivated alternative are partly supported in safety suppression with utility retention, but title/abstract generality about faithful bi-directional steering outruns the mixed, factor-tuned AXBENCH evidence.

significance.justification: Steering–interpretability crossover and utility-preserving safety interventions would interest ICLR readers, but impact is tempered by mixed general-purpose results versus strong existing optimizers like RePS.

novelty.justification: JSD full-vocabulary matching plus DII for bi-directional steering is a genuine twist, yet it is largely a recombination of DAS-style interventions and distillation-style distribution matching rather than a new paradigm.

rigor.justification: Equations and protocols are mostly sound, but claim–evidence links are uneven: faithfulness is partly operationalized via KL/utility, while general steering superiority and causal grounding remain under-supported.

statistical_soundness.justification: Fair AXBENCH splits and three-seed backdoor curves with SE help, but most tables lack multi-seed variance and formal significance, and tinyBenchmarks underpower utility conclusions.

calibration_honesty.justification: The paper repeatedly notes it does not always outperform Lang./PO, reports oracle vs fair scores, and states limitations on data, tuning, rank, and causal theory—above typical borderline honesty.

clarity.justification: Structure and intuition are followable and equations are given, but dense notation, overloaded “DAS” naming, and compressed experimental protocols reduce precision for non-specialists.

structure_compliance.justification: Standard ICLR flow is present (Intro, Related Work, Method, AXBENCH, case studies, Conclusion) at a reasonable conference length with clear section roles.

reproducibility.justification: Ignoring redacted links, data construction, objectives, intervention forms, factor policies, layers, and evaluation judges are described sufficiently to attempt reproduction, though some details live in unshown appendices.

related_work.justification: Steering objectives, DAS/localization, distillation/JSD, and refusal/backdoor probes are discussed with a clear complementary claim, but comparison fairness and boundary vs. DAS could be sharper.

figure_quality.justification: Captions describe informative comparisons (AXBENCH scores, refusal metrics, utility/KL, layer-wise ASR with error bands) that directly support the main empirical claims rather than decorate them.

breadth_generality.justification: General steering is only on Gemma-2 2B/9B with layer-sensitive outcomes; case studies help but do not rescue under-supported generality for “faithful bi-directional steering” as a broad method.

overall_recommendation.justification: Borderline reject at ICLR: interesting and partly validated in safety settings, but mixed primary-benchmark evidence, incomplete ablations, and uneven tuning protocols need substantial revision before acceptance.
